name: CSS
description: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is used to style and design web pages.

blocks.html:
Introduction to CSS (Cascading Style Sheets)

CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) is a stylesheet language used to describe the presentation of a document written in HTML or XML. While HTML provides the structure and content of a webpage, CSS controls the visual appearance and layout of that content, including colors, fonts, spacing, positioning, animations, and responsiveness.

CSS is a cornerstone technology of the World Wide Web, alongside HTML and JavaScript. It enables web developers and designers to create visually engaging and user-friendly websites.

Why CSS is Important

  • Separation of Content and Presentation: Keeps HTML structure clean and CSS handles design separately.
  • Consistency Across Pages: Apply the same styles to multiple pages for a uniform look.
  • Improved Accessibility: Adjust how content is presented for different devices and users, including those with disabilities.
  • Responsive Design: Make websites adapt to screens like desktops, tablets, and mobile devices.
  • Performance: External CSS files are cached by browsers, improving page load speed.

How CSS Works: The Cascade and Specificity

The term "Cascading" in CSS refers to how styles are applied when multiple rules target the same element. The browser determines which style to apply using:

  • Importance: Rules with !important override others.
  • Specificity: IDs override classes, which override element selectors.
  • Source Order: If specificity is equal, the last rule in the file wins.

CSS Syntax

A CSS rule consists of two main parts:

  1. Selector: Specifies which HTML element(s) the rule applies to. Examples: p, .class, #id.
  2. Declaration Block: Enclosed in curly braces { }, containing property-value pairs.

Example:

h1 {
    color: #333333;
    font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
    font-size: 36px;
    margin-bottom: 20px;
}

This rule styles all <h1> elements with:

  • Dark gray text color (#333333).
  • Arial font, or generic sans-serif if Arial is unavailable.
  • Font size of 36px.
  • Margin of 20px below the heading.

Types of CSS

There are three primary ways to include CSS in HTML:

1. Inline CSS

Inline CSS is applied directly to an HTML element using the style attribute. 

<p style="color: blue; font-size: 14px;">This is a blue paragraph.</p>

Output:

This is a blue paragraph.

2. Internal CSS

Internal CSS is written inside a <style> tag within the <head> section of an HTML document. 

<head>
    <style>
        p {
            color: green;
            font-size: 18px;
        }
    </style>
</head>
<body>
    <p>This paragraph uses internal CSS.</p>
</body>

Output:

This paragraph uses internal CSS.

3. External CSS

External CSS is stored in a separate .css file and linked to the HTML using the <link> tag. 

<head>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">
</head>

styles.css

p {
    color: red;
    font-size: 20px;
}

Output (Simulated):

This paragraph uses external CSS.

Common CSS Properties

  • Color and Background: color, background-color, background-image, background-size
  • Text and Fonts: font-family, font-size, font-weight, line-height, text-align, text-decoration
  • Box Model: margin, padding, border, width, height
  • Layout: display, position, float, top, left
  • Flexbox: display: flex, justify-content, align-items, flex-direction

Live Example: Styled Card

Below is a live example of using CSS to style a card:

<div class="card">
    <h3>CSS Card</h3>
    <p>This is a beautifully styled card using CSS.</p>
</div>

<style>
.card {
    border: 1px solid #ccc;
    padding: 15px;
    border-radius: 10px;
    background-color: #f9f9f9;
    width: 250px;
    text-align: center;
}
.card h3 {
    color: #333;
}
</style>

Output:

CSS Card

This is a beautifully styled card using CSS.

Summary

CSS is a powerful tool that brings HTML content to life. By mastering CSS, you can create visually appealing, responsive, and accessible websites. Start small, learn the basic properties, and gradually move to advanced concepts like Flexbox and Grid.

topics.title: Selectors

blocks.html:
CSS Selectors

CSS selectors are patterns used to target HTML elements for styling. They allow you to apply styles to specific elements or groups of elements in a webpage. Understanding selectors is essential for writing clean, efficient, and scalable CSS.

Types of CSS Selectors

CSS selectors can be grouped into the following main categories:

  • Basic Selectors - Target elements by name, class, or ID.
  • Combinator Selectors - Define relationships between elements.
  • Group Selectors - Apply the same style to multiple elements.
  • Pseudo-classes - Target elements in specific states (e.g., hover).
  • Pseudo-elements - Style specific parts of an element (e.g., first letter).
  • Attribute Selectors - Select elements based on attributes.

1. Basic Selectors

Basic selectors are the most commonly used in CSS.

Example Code:

/* Element Selector */
p {
    color: blue;
}

/* Class Selector */
.highlight {
    background-color: yellow;
    font-weight: bold;
}

/* ID Selector */
#unique-title {
    color: red;
    text-decoration: underline;
}

Live Output:

This is a normal paragraph.

This paragraph uses a class selector.

This heading uses an ID selector.

2. Group Selectors

Group selectors allow you to apply the same style to multiple elements by separating them with a comma.

h2, h3, p {
    color: green;
    font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
}

Live Output:

Heading 2 styled with group selector

Heading 3 styled with group selector

Paragraph styled with group selector

3. Combinator Selectors

Combinators define relationships between elements.

  • Descendant (space): Targets elements nested inside another.
  • Child (>): Targets direct children only.
  • Adjacent (+): Targets the element immediately after another.
  • General sibling (~): Targets all siblings after another element.
/* Descendant */
div p {
    color: blue;
}

/* Child */
div > p {
    font-weight: bold;
}

/* Adjacent */
h4 + p {
    color: red;
}

/* General Sibling */
h4 ~ p {
    font-style: italic;
}

Live Output:

Title

This paragraph is directly after H4 (Adjacent selector applied).

Another sibling paragraph (General sibling selector applied).

Nested paragraph inside a div (Descendant & Child applied).

4. Attribute Selectors

Attribute selectors target elements based on their attributes or attribute values.

/* Elements with title attribute */
[title] {
    color: purple;
}

/* Specific attribute value */
[type="text"] {
    border: 2px solid blue;
}

/* Attribute value starts with */
[href^="https"] {
    color: green;
}

/* Attribute value ends with */
[href$=".pdf"] {
    color: red;
}

/* Attribute value contains */
[class*="btn"] {
    background-color: orange;
    color: white;
}

Live Output:

This paragraph has a title attribute.

HTTPS link

PDF link

5. Pseudo-classes

Pseudo-classes style elements in a specific state like hover or focus.

a:hover {
    color: red;
    text-decoration: underline;
}

input:focus {
    border: 2px solid green;
}

li:first-child {
    font-weight: bold;
}

li:last-child {
    color: blue;
}

Live Output:

Hover over this link



  • First Item (first-child styled)
  • Middle Item
  • Last Item (last-child styled)

6. Pseudo-elements

Pseudo-elements allow you to style specific parts of an element.

p::first-letter {
    font-size: 24px;
    color: red;
}

p::first-line {
    font-weight: bold;
}

p::selection {
    background: yellow;
    color: black;
}

Live Output:

Select this text to see the ::selection effect. Notice the first letter and first line styling.

Summary

  • Basic selectors: Target by element, class, or ID.
  • Group selectors: Apply styles to multiple elements at once.
  • Combinators: Define parent-child or sibling relationships.
  • Attribute selectors: Target elements with specific attributes or values.
  • Pseudo-classes: Style based on states like hover or focus.
  • Pseudo-elements: Style specific parts of an element.

topics.title: Specificity & Inheritance

blocks.html:
CSS Specificity & Inheritance

Introduction to CSS Specificity

CSS specificity determines which CSS rule is applied when multiple rules target the same element. It is an essential concept in CSS because when you write styles, sometimes two or more rules may conflict.

The browser uses specificity to resolve conflicts and decide which style takes precedence.

Why Specificity is Important

  • Helps you predict which style will be applied to an element.
  • Prevents confusion and unexpected styling issues.
  • Encourages writing cleaner and maintainable code.
  • Avoids overusing !important, which can make CSS hard to manage.

How Specificity is Calculated

Specificity is calculated based on four levels of selectors. You can think of them like a scoring system:

Selector Type Example Weight Description
Inline Styles <h1 style="color: red;"> 1000 Highest priority - styles written directly on the element.
ID Selectors #header { } 100 Each ID in a selector adds 100 points.
Class, Pseudo-class, Attribute Selectors .title { } or :hover 10 Each class or pseudo-class adds 10 points.
Element Selectors div { }, p { } 1 Each HTML tag adds 1 point.
Universal Selector & Combinators *, +, > 0 Do not add any points to specificity.

When comparing rules, the rule with the higher score wins. If two rules have the same score, the later rule in the CSS file takes precedence.

Specificity Example

Let's consider this HTML:

<p class="highlight" id="special">This is a paragraph</p>

CSS Rules:

p {
    color: blue;           /* Score = 1 */
}

.highlight {
    color: green;          /* Score = 10 */
}

#special {
    color: red;            /* Score = 100 */
}

p#special {
    color: orange;         /* Score = 101 */
}

The final color of the paragraph will be orange because p#special has the highest specificity score.

Live Output:

This is a paragraph styled with different specificity levels.

The !important Rule

The !important rule overrides all other rules, regardless of specificity. It should be used sparingly because it can make your CSS harder to debug and maintain. 

p {
    color: blue !important;
}

#special {
    color: red;
}

In this case, the paragraph will be blue, even though the ID selector is usually stronger.

This paragraph is styled with !important.

CSS Inheritance

CSS Inheritance is the mechanism by which some CSS properties are automatically passed from parent elements to their child elements. This behavior helps maintain consistency and reduces repetitive code.

How Inheritance Works:

  • Child elements automatically inherit certain styles from their parent, such as color, font-family, and line-height.
  • Other properties, like margin, padding, border, and background, do not inherit by default.
Example:
<div class="parent">
    <p>This is a child paragraph</p>
    <span>This is a child span</span>
</div>

CSS:

.parent {
    color: green;
    font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
}

p {
    font-size: 18px;
}

In this example:

  • The text color of both the paragraph and span will be green because color is inheritable.
  • The font-size only applies to the paragraph because it is explicitly set there.

Live Output:

This is a child paragraph

This is a child span

Controlling Inheritance with Keywords:

  • inherit → Forces a property to inherit from its parent.
  • initial → Resets a property to its default value.
  • unset → Acts as inherit if the property is normally inheritable; otherwise, it acts as initial.
p {
    color: inherit; /* Force color to be inherited */
    background-color: initial; /* Reset background to default */
}

Best Practices for Specificity & Inheritance

  • Keep your CSS as flat as possible. Avoid deeply nested selectors.
  • Use classes for styling instead of IDs for flexibility and reuse.
  • Only use !important when absolutely necessary.
  • Understand which properties are inheritable to reduce repetitive code.
  • Organize stylesheets so more specific rules are written later.

Summary

  • Specificity decides which CSS rule is applied when multiple rules target the same element.
  • Inline styles > IDs > Classes > Elements.
  • Universal selectors and combinators do not add specificity weight.
  • Inheritance allows certain styles to flow from parent to child automatically.
  • !important overrides all specificity calculations.
  • Use inheritance wisely to keep your CSS clean and efficient.

topics.title: Box Model

blocks.html:
CSS Box Model

The CSS Box Model is a crucial concept for web design and layout. It defines how every element on a webpage is structured in terms of content, padding, border, and margin. By understanding it, you can control spacing, alignment, and sizing effectively.

Box Model Breakdown

Each HTML element can be thought of as a box consisting of the following layers:

  • Content: The actual content like text or images.
  • Padding: Space between the content and border.
  • Border: A visible edge surrounding the padding.
  • Margin: Space outside the border, separating this element from others.

Live Demo of Box Model

Hover over the box below to visualize each part of the box model clearly.

Content Area

Explanation:

  • Content (white area): Text "Content Area".
  • Padding (light blue): Space around the text inside the box.
  • Border (dark blue): The thick outline around the padding.
  • Margin (orange): Space outside the border separating this box from surrounding elements.

Example Code


.box-content {
    padding: 20px;            /* Padding: space between content and border */
    border: 5px solid #0056b3; /* Border: outline of the box */
    margin: 30px;              /* Margin: space outside the border */
    background-color: #ffffff; /* Background for content area */
}

Box Sizing Property

By default, width and height only include the content area. Padding and border are added on top, making the final box larger.

The box-sizing property changes this behavior:

  • content-box (default): width = content only.
  • border-box: width includes content, padding, and border.
Content-Box
Border-Box

/* Default box-sizing */
.content-box {
    box-sizing: content-box;
    width: 200px;
    padding: 20px;
    border: 5px solid blue;
}

/* Border-box sizing */
.border-box {
    box-sizing: border-box;
    width: 200px;
    padding: 20px;
    border: 5px solid green;
}

topics.title: Color, Background & Typography

blocks.html:
CSS Colors, Backgrounds, and Typography

These three concepts are the foundation of visually engaging web design. They control how a website looks, how readable the text is, and how the overall user experience feels.

1. CSS Colors

CSS colors define how text, backgrounds, borders, and other elements appear visually. You can define colors in different ways such as Named Colors, HEX Codes, RGB, RGBA, HSL, and HSLA.

Different Ways to Define Colors:

  • Named Colors: e.g., color: red;
  • HEX Codes: e.g., color: #ff0000;
  • RGB: e.g., color: rgb(255,0,0);
  • RGBA: e.g., color: rgba(255,0,0,0.5); (with transparency)
  • HSL: e.g., color: hsl(0,100%,50%);
  • HSLA: e.g., color: hsla(0,100%,50%,0.5);

Live Demo:

This text uses a named color (red).

This text uses a HEX color (#3498db).

This text uses an RGB color.

This text uses RGBA color (semi-transparent red).

This text uses an HSL color.

2. CSS Backgrounds

Backgrounds improve the visual depth of web elements. You can set solid colors, images, or gradient backgrounds.

Background Properties:

  • background-color - Sets a solid color.
  • background-image - Adds a background image.
  • background-repeat - Controls repetition of background images.
  • background-size - `cover`, `contain`, or custom dimensions.
  • background-position - Defines image placement.
  • background-attachment - `scroll` or `fixed` for parallax effects.
  • linear-gradient - Creates smooth color transitions.

Live Demo:

Solid Color Background
Image Background
Gradient Background

3. CSS Typography

Typography controls how text looks and feels on a webpage. It impacts readability, aesthetics, and user engagement.

Common Typography Properties:

  • font-family - Defines the font style.
  • font-size - Sets text size.
  • font-weight - `normal`, `bold`, `lighter`, or numeric (100-900).
  • font-style - `normal`, `italic`, or `oblique`.
  • text-align - Aligns text (`left`, `center`, `right`, `justify`).
  • text-transform - `uppercase`, `lowercase`, `capitalize`.
  • line-height - Vertical spacing between lines.
  • letter-spacing - Horizontal spacing between letters.
  • word-spacing - Horizontal spacing between words.
  • text-decoration - `underline`, `line-through`, `none`.

Live Demo:

This text uses a custom font family with fallbacks.

This text demonstrates different font sizes.

This text is bold using font-weight.

This text is italic using font-style.

this text is transformed to uppercase.

This text has extra letter and word spacing.

Summary

  • Colors: Control the visual mood and hierarchy of elements.
  • Backgrounds: Enhance depth using images, colors, and gradients.
  • Typography: Ensures readability, clarity, and aesthetic harmony.

By mastering these concepts, you can create visually appealing and accessible web pages that engage users and improve the overall design.

CSS Layout

Introduction to CSS Layout

CSS Layout defines how elements are displayed, positioned, and structured on a webpage. A good understanding of layout helps you build responsive and user-friendly designs.

  • Arrange elements like headers, sidebars, and content areas.
  • Control how elements interact with each other.
  • Create responsive designs for different screen sizes.

1. Display Property

The display property determines how an element is shown on the page.

Value Description
blockStarts on a new line and takes full width (e.g., <div>).
inlineStays inline with other content without starting a new line (e.g., <span>).
inline-blockBehaves like inline but allows setting width and height.
noneCompletely hides the element.
Example Code:
.block-example {
    display: block;
    background: lightblue;
    margin-bottom: 10px;
}

.inline-example {
    display: inline;
    background: lightgreen;
    padding: 5px;
}

.inline-block-example {
    display: inline-block;
    background: lightcoral;
    width: 100px;
    height: 50px;
    text-align: center;
}
Live Output:
Block Element
Inline 1 Inline 2
Inline-Block

2. Positioning

The position property controls how an element is placed on the page. There are five main values:

  • static - Default behavior, normal document flow.
  • relative - Positioned relative to its normal position.
  • absolute - Positioned relative to the nearest positioned ancestor.
  • fixed - Stays fixed in place even when scrolling.
  • sticky - Switches between relative and fixed depending on scroll position.
Example Code:
.relative-box {
    position: relative;
    top: 10px;
    left: 20px;
    background: lightyellow;
}

.absolute-box {
    position: absolute;
    top: 30px;
    left: 50px;
    background: lightpink;
}

.fixed-box {
    position: fixed;
    bottom: 10px;
    right: 10px;
    background: lightgreen;
    padding: 5px;
}

.sticky-box {
    position: sticky;
    top: 0;
    background: orange;
}
Live Output:
Relative Box
Absolute Box
Sticky Header (scroll to test)
Fixed Box

3. Flexbox Basics

Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout model that helps align and distribute elements inside a container efficiently, either horizontally or vertically.

Important Flexbox Properties:

  • Container Properties:
    • display: flex; - Enables Flexbox.
    • flex-direction - Row or column layout.
    • justify-content - Alignment along main axis.
    • align-items - Alignment along cross axis.
    • gap - Space between flex items.
  • Item Properties:
    • flex - Defines how items grow or shrink.
    • align-self - Overrides container alignment for a single item.
Example Code:
.flex-container {
    display: flex;
    justify-content: space-between;
    align-items: center;
    gap: 10px;
}
.flex-item {
    background: lightblue;
    padding: 20px;
    text-align: center;
    flex: 1;
}
Live Output:
Item 1
Item 2
Item 3

4. Grid Basics

CSS Grid is a two-dimensional layout system, perfect for designing layouts with rows and columns.

Important Grid Properties:

  • display: grid; - Enables grid layout.
  • grid-template-columns - Defines number and size of columns.
  • grid-template-rows - Defines number and size of rows.
  • gap - Space between grid cells.
  • grid-column and grid-row - Position individual items.
Example Code:
.grid-container {
    display: grid;
    grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr);
    gap: 10px;
}
.grid-item {
    background: #3498db;
    color: white;
    text-align: center;
    padding: 20px;
}

Summary

  • Display Property: Controls how elements are rendered (block, inline, etc.).
  • Positioning: Precisely controls element placement.
  • Flexbox: One-dimensional layouts (rows or columns).
  • Grid: Two-dimensional layouts (rows and columns).

Mastering these layout techniques allows you to create modern, responsive, and well-structured websites.

topics.title: Flexbox in Depth

blocks.html:
Flexbox in Depth

The Big Idea

Flexbox lays out items in one direction at a time (a row or a column) and makes it easy to align, space and resize them. Put display: flex on the container; its direct children become flex items.

.container {
  display: flex;
}

Flexbox has two axes: the main axis (the direction items flow, a row by default) and the cross axis (perpendicular to it). justify-content works on the main axis, align-items on the cross axis.

Container Properties

PropertyWhat it doesCommon values
flex-directionSets the main axisrow, column
justify-contentSpaces items along the main axisflex-start, center, space-between, space-around
align-itemsAligns items on the cross axisstretch, center, flex-start
flex-wrapLets items wrap onto new linesnowrap, wrap
gapSpace between items10px, 1rem

justify-content: space-between

1
2
3

Perfect centering (the classic Flexbox trick):

Centered
.container {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: center; /* horizontal */
  align-items: center;     /* vertical */
  height: 200px;
}

Item Properties

PropertyMeaning
flex-growHow much extra space an item takes (0 = none)
flex-shrinkHow much an item may shrink when space is tight
flex-basisStarting size before growing or shrinking
flexShorthand: flex: 1 means grow equally
align-selfOverride align-items for one item
orderChange the visual order

The middle item has flex-grow: 2 (it gets twice the extra space):

  flex-grow: 2;
}

Wrapping

By default items squeeze onto one line. Use flex-wrap: wrap so they move to the next line when there is no room. Resize your window to see it.

A Real Example: Navigation Bar

nav {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: space-between;
  align-items: center;
  padding: 0 20px;
}
nav ul {
  display: flex;
  gap: 16px;
  list-style: none;
}

The logo sits on the left, the links on the right, and everything is vertically centered. This is exactly how the Learning Hub navbar works.

topics.title: CSS Grid in Depth

blocks.html:
CSS Grid in Depth

The Big Idea

CSS Grid lays out items in rows and columns at the same time. Use it for whole-page layouts, galleries and dashboards. Put display: grid on the container and describe the columns.

.grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr 1fr; /* three equal columns */
  gap: 12px;
}
1
2
3
4
5
6

The fr unit means "a fraction of the free space". repeat(3, 1fr) is a shorter way to write the same thing.

Responsive Grid Without Media Queries

.cards {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(160px, 1fr));
  gap: 12px;
}

This single line says: "make as many columns as fit, each at least 160px wide, and share the leftover space." Resize the window and watch the columns change:

Placing and Spanning Items

.wide {
  grid-column: span 2;   /* take two columns */
}
.tall {
  grid-row: span 2;      /* take two rows */
}

Named Areas

You can draw your layout with words:

.page {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 150px 1fr;
  grid-template-areas:
    "header header"
    "sidebar content"
    "footer footer";
  gap: 10px;
}
.page header  { grid-area: header; }
.page aside   { grid-area: sidebar; }
.page main    { grid-area: content; }
.page footer  { grid-area: footer; }

Starts fromThe contentThe layout

They work great together: Grid for the page, Flexbox inside each piece.

CSS Spacing & Responsive Design

Introduction

Spacing and responsive design are essential in creating clean, readable, and user-friendly web layouts. Proper use of margin, padding, and responsive units ensures that your website looks great on all devices and screen sizes.

1. Spacing - Margin and Padding

In CSS, margin and padding are used to create space around elements.

  • Margin: Space outside an element's border.
  • Padding: Space inside an element's border, between the content and the border.
Example Code:
.box {
    background: lightblue;
    margin: 20px;      /* Adds space outside the box */
    padding: 15px;     /* Adds space inside the box */
}
Live Output:
This box has 20px margin and 15px padding.

2. Shorthand Properties for Margin and Padding

You can use shorthand syntax for setting margins or padding for all sides of an element in a single line:

Syntax Description
margin: 10px;All sides are 10px.
margin: 10px 20px;Top/Bottom = 10px, Left/Right = 20px.
margin: 10px 20px 30px;Top = 10px, Left/Right = 20px, Bottom = 30px.
margin: 10px 20px 30px 40px;Top = 10px, Right = 20px, Bottom = 30px, Left = 40px (clockwise).
Live Output:
margin: 10px;
margin: 10px 20px;
margin: 10px 20px 30px;
margin: 10px 20px 30px 40px;

3. Responsive Design

Responsive design ensures your website adjusts gracefully to different screen sizes and devices like desktops, tablets, and smartphones.

3.1 Media Queries Basics

Media queries let you apply styles only when certain conditions (like screen width) are met. 

@media (max-width: 600px) {
    body {
        background-color: lightblue;
    }
}

In this example, when the screen width is 600px or less, the background color will change to light blue.

Live Demo:

Resize the browser window below 600px to see the effect.

This box will change color on smaller screens (under 600px width).

3.2 Relative Units

Relative units scale elements based on factors like parent size or viewport size:

  • em - Relative to the font size of the element.
  • rem - Relative to the root font size (usually the <html> element).
  • % - Percentage relative to the parent element's size.
  • vh - Relative to 1% of the viewport height.
  • vw - Relative to 1% of the viewport width.
Example Code:
.relative-example {
    font-size: 1.5em;   /* 1.5 times the parent font size */
    padding: 2rem;      /* 2 times the root font size */
    width: 50%;         /* 50% of parent width */
    height: 20vh;       /* 20% of the viewport height */
}
Live Output:
Responsive Box using em, rem, %, vh

Summary

  • Margin & Padding: Control spacing outside and inside elements.
  • Shorthand Properties: Set multiple sides' spacing in a single line.
  • Media Queries: Adapt styles for different screen sizes.
  • Relative Units: Make layouts flexible and scalable.

Combining proper spacing with responsive design techniques creates clean, scalable, and mobile-friendly websites.

topics.title: Pseudo-class & Pseudo-Element

blocks.html:
CSS Pseudo-Classes & Pseudo-Elements

Introduction

CSS pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements are special selectors that allow you to style elements based on their state, position, or specific parts of their content without needing extra HTML elements.

They are incredibly useful for creating dynamic and interactive user interfaces. With pseudo-classes, you can style elements when a user hovers, clicks, or when an element is in a specific state. Pseudo-elements allow you to style specific parts of elements or even insert content dynamically.

Difference Between Pseudo-Classes and Pseudo-Elements

Aspect Pseudo-Class Pseudo-Element
Definition Defines a state or condition of an element. Styles a specific part of an element or adds content.
Syntax Uses a : (single colon) → Example: :hover Uses :: (double colon) → Example: ::before
Example Change button color on hover → button:hover Add an icon before text → p::before
Purpose Interactivity and conditional styling Content manipulation and fine-grained styling

1. CSS Pseudo-Classes

A pseudo-class targets elements based on their **state** or **relationship with other elements**. It does not change the DOM structure; it just applies styles conditionally.

Common Pseudo-Classes:

  • :hover - When the user hovers over an element.
  • :focus - When an element is focused (e.g., an input field).
  • :active - When an element is actively being clicked.
  • :first-child - Targets the first child inside a parent.
  • :last-child - Targets the last child inside a parent.
  • :nth-child(n) - Targets specific children based on position.
  • :not(selector) - Selects everything except the specified selector.
  • :checked - When a checkbox or radio button is selected.
Example Code:
a:hover {
    color: red;
    text-decoration: underline;
}

input:focus {
    border: 2px solid green;
}

li:first-child {
    font-weight: bold;
}

li:last-child {
    color: blue;
}

li:nth-child(2) {
    background-color: lightyellow;
}
Live Output:
Hover over this link



  • First Item
  • Second Item
  • Third Item

2. CSS Pseudo-Elements

A pseudo-element styles **specific parts** of an element or adds **virtual elements** without changing the actual HTML. Think of it as creating a sub-element purely with CSS.

Common Pseudo-Elements:

  • ::first-letter - Styles the first letter of a text block.
  • ::first-line - Styles the first line of a text block.
  • ::before - Inserts content before an element.
  • ::after - Inserts content after an element.
  • ::selection - Styles text when the user highlights it.
Example Code:
p::first-letter {
    font-size: 24px;
    color: red;
}

p::first-line {
    font-weight: bold;
}

p::selection {
    background: yellow;
    color: black;
}

.box::before {
    content: "Start - ";
    color: green;
}

.box::after {
    content: " - End";
    color: blue;
}
Live Output:

Select this text to see the ::selection effect. Notice the first letter and first line styling.

This is a div with ::before and ::after applied.

3. Combining Pseudo-Classes and Pseudo-Elements

You can combine both pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements to create **interactive and styled elements**. Here, we create a button that changes color on hover and adds an arrow dynamically.

Example Code:
.button {
    position: relative;
    padding: 10px 20px;
    background: #07284dff;
    color: white;
    border: none;
    cursor: pointer;
    font-size: 16px;
    border-radius: 5px;
}

.button:hover {
    background: #162d46ff;
}

.button::after {
    content: " →";
    position: absolute;
    right: 10px;
}
Live Output:

Best Practices

  • Use pseudo-classes for interaction states like hover, focus, and active.
  • Use pseudo-elements to insert decorative content or highlight specific text parts.
  • Keep content meaningful. Do not insert important information with pseudo-elements, as it won't be accessible to screen readers.
  • Scope your styles to prevent affecting other parts of your site.
  • Remember that ::before and ::after require the content property, even if it's empty.

Summary

  • Pseudo-Classes style elements based on their state or position, like :hover or :first-child.
  • Pseudo-Elements style specific parts of elements or add content dynamically, like ::before and ::after.
  • Together, they provide a powerful, flexible system for designing interactive, user-friendly websites.

topics.title: Transitions & Animations

blocks.html:
Transitions & Animations

Transitions: Smooth Changes

Normally a hover effect changes instantly. A transition makes the change happen smoothly over time.

.btn {
  background: #38bdf8;
  transition: background 0.3s ease, transform 0.3s ease;
}
.btn:hover {
  background: #f97316;
  transform: scale(1.08);
}

Hover over the button:

Hover me

The transition shorthand is: property duration timing-function delay.

Timing Functions

ValueFeel
easeStarts slow, speeds up, ends slow (default)
linearSame speed all the way
ease-inStarts slow
ease-outEnds slow
ease-in-outSlow at both ends

Transform

transform moves, resizes or rotates an element without disturbing the layout around it. It is also very smooth for the browser.

FunctionExample
translate()transform: translateX(20px)
scale()transform: scale(1.2)
rotate()transform: rotate(15deg)

Hover to rotate and grow:

Hover me

Keyframe Animations

When you need something that moves on its own (not only on hover), describe the steps with @keyframes and apply them with animation.

@keyframes bounce {
  0%, 100% { transform: translateY(0); }
  50%      { transform: translateY(-20px); }
}

.ball {
  animation: bounce 1s ease-in-out infinite;
}
PropertyMeaning
animation-nameWhich @keyframes to use
animation-durationHow long one run takes
animation-iteration-countHow many times (infinite for forever)
animation-delayWait before starting
animation-fill-modeKeep the first/last frame (forwards)

Good Animation Habits

  • Animate transform and opacity. They are cheap for the browser. Avoid animating width, height or top.
  • Keep it short: 150 to 400 ms feels responsive.
  • Animate to help the user (show what changed), not just to decorate.
  • Respect people who ask for less motion:
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  * {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
  }
}

Learning Hub uses exactly this rule, so the demos above stay still for users who turned motion off in their system settings.

topics.title: Variables, Units & Modern Functions

blocks.html:
CSS Variables & Units

Custom Properties (Variables)

A CSS variable stores a value once so you can reuse it everywhere. Names start with two dashes and you read them with var().

:root {
  --brand: #38bdf8;
  --radius: 12px;
}

.button {
  background: var(--brand);
  border-radius: var(--radius);
}
.card {
  border: 2px solid var(--brand);
  border-radius: var(--radius);
}

Change --brand in one place and the whole site updates. :root means "the whole page".

Variables Can Be Overridden

A variable can be replaced inside a smaller area. Both boxes below use the same rule, but the second one overrides --accent:

.box { background: var(--accent, gray); }   /* gray is the fallback */
.box.orange { --accent: #f97316; }
Default accent
Overridden accent

Dark Mode in a Few Lines

:root {
  --bg: #ffffff;
  --text: #0f172a;
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root {
    --bg: #0f172a;
    --text: #e2e8f0;
  }
}
body {
  background: var(--bg);
  color: var(--text);
}

Units You Will Actually Use

UnitRelative toUse for
pxFixed screen pixelBorders, small details
remRoot font size (usually 16px)Font sizes, spacing (accessible)
emFont size of the element itselfPadding that scales with text
%The parent's sizeWidths inside containers
vw / vh1% of window width / heightFull-screen sections
chWidth of the "0" characterComfortable text width (max-width: 65ch)

Prefer rem for font sizes so the text grows when the user increases their browser font size.

calc(), min(), max() and clamp()

.sidebar { width: calc(100% - 250px); }
.photo   { width: min(100%, 600px); }   /* never wider than 600px */
.title   { font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 4vw, 3rem); }
  • calc() does maths with mixed units.
  • min() / max() pick the smaller or larger value.
  • clamp(min, preferred, max) is perfect for fluid text that grows with the screen but never gets too small or too big.
